fields.description: Anger wounds those we love and shames us. Here is how to overcome it — dealing with its roots, being slow to speak, forgiving, and putting on the gentleness of Christ.
fields.body_html:
Anger is one of the most common and destructive struggles of the human heart. A flash of temper can wound those we love most, ruin relationships built over years, and leave us ashamed of ourselves. For many Christians it is a besetting sin they battle in secret, wondering why they cannot master it. The good news is that no one has to stay a prisoner of their temper. Scripture speaks directly and hopefully to anger — not merely telling us to suppress it, but showing us where it comes from, how to deal with its roots, and how, by God’s grace, to grow in the gentleness of Christ. This is not a quick fix but a real and lasting change that God is willing to work in anyone who will cooperate with him. “Know this, my beloved brothers: let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger; for the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:19–20). Here is how to overcome it.

Not all anger is sinful — but ours usually is

First, a clarification that brings both relief and challenge: not all anger is sin. God himself is angry at evil, and Jesus was rightly angry at hardness of heart and the abuse of the temple. There is a righteous anger against injustice and sin. But we must be honest: most of our anger is not this pure, God-honouring kind. Ours is usually provoked by wounded pride, thwarted desires, or personal offence — anger for our own sake, not God’s.

That is why Scripture handles our anger so carefully: “Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger, and give no opportunity to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). Even where anger begins rightly, it easily curdles into sin, resentment, and a foothold for the enemy. So the goal is not to feel nothing, but to be freed from the selfish, sinful anger that damages us and others — and honesty about which kind is ours is the first step.

Understand where anger comes from

To overcome anger, we must look beneath the surface, for anger is a symptom before it is the disease. James asks pointedly where our quarrels come from, and answers: from our own cravings, our unmet desires, our demands that life and people give us what we want (James 4:1–2). Anger flares when something we love or want — comfort, respect, control, our own way — is threatened or denied. It is often a window into our idols: what we get angriest about reveals what we most love and trust apart from God.

This is actually hopeful, because it tells us where the real work is. Merely gritting our teeth to hold our temper treats the symptom; the cure is deeper — dealing with the cravings and demands underneath. When we bring those to God, loosen our grip on our rights, and let him be our security and satisfaction, the fuel for much of our anger is removed. Anger managed at the surface will keep erupting; anger addressed at the root begins to lose its power.

Be slow — put space between the spark and the response

Much sinful anger does its damage in the first hot seconds, so Scripture repeatedly counsels slowness. “Whoever is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who has a hasty temper exalts folly” (Proverbs 14:29). “A fool gives full vent to his spirit, but a wise man quietly holds it back” (Proverbs 29:11). The wisdom here is intensely practical: put space between the provocation and your response. Pause. Breathe. Pray before you speak. Do not fire off the angry word or message in the heat of the moment.

And guard your words above all, for the tongue is where anger does its worst. “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Learning to give a soft answer — to lower your voice rather than raise it, to respond gently rather than sharply — can defuse a conflict before it explodes. The Psalmist’s counsel is a good habit for the angry heart: “Be angry, and do not sin; ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent” (Psalm 4:4). Silence and reflection, rather than instant reaction, are the friends of a peaceable heart.

Put anger to death and put on gentleness

The Christian is called not merely to manage anger but to put it off entirely as part of the old life. “But now you must put them all away: anger, wrath, malice, slander, and obscene talk from your mouth” (Colossians 3:8). This is the language of decisive removal — taking off a filthy garment. The old writers on holiness spoke of the daily work of putting sin to death by the Spirit, and anger is exactly the kind of sin that must be actively mortified, not merely apologized for again and again.

But Scripture never leaves us with only a negative. We put anger off in order to put something better on: “Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32). The fruit of the Spirit includes “patience, kindness... gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23), and these grow in us as we walk with God. Overcoming anger, then, is not just emptying the heart of rage but filling it with the gentleness of Christ — replacing the reflex to lash out with a growing reflex to be patient, kind, and quick to forgive.

Forgive, and leave justice to God

Much anger is really unforgiveness — a grievance nursed and rehearsed until it hardens into bitterness. The antidote is forgiveness: releasing the offender and leaving the matter with God. “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord’” (Romans 12:19). We can let go of our anger because God is the just Judge; we do not have to hold the scales ourselves.

This is where the gospel does its deepest work on our anger. When we remember how much God has forgiven us — an unpayable debt, cancelled at the cross — the offences we cling to shrink to their true size. A heart amazed by grace becomes a heart quick to extend it. Jesus warned that unchecked anger against a brother is a grave matter (Matthew 5:22), precisely because he means to make us people of mercy. The more we drink from the forgiveness we have received, the more freely it flows out of us toward others.

When you have already sinned in anger

What do we do after we have lost our temper — said the cutting word, sent the angry message, wounded someone we love? Here too the gospel gives a way forward that neither excuses the sin nor leaves us in despair. The first step is honest confession to God, who forgives. The second is to go and make it right with the person we wronged. Jesus put reconciliation ahead of even religious duty: “if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you... first be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew 5:23–24).

A humble, specific apology — owning the wrong without excuses, without the word “but” — does more to heal a relationship and to humble a proud heart than almost anything else. It also breaks the grip of anger, because pride is anger’s fuel, and there is little so contrary to pride as saying, “I was wrong; please forgive me.” Do not let shame keep you from it. Every honest repair, though painful, is a step toward becoming the gentle person God is making you, and God delights to meet us in that humility with fresh grace.

Depend on grace, and don’t give up

Overcoming anger is the work of a lifetime, and it is done in dependence on God, not by willpower alone. Ask him daily for a gentle heart and the Spirit’s self-control. When you fail — and you will, at times — confess it quickly, make it right with those you wounded, and get back up. Do not let a defeat become despair; the very grief you feel over your temper is a sign the Spirit is at work.

Take heart that God is patient with us as we learn to be patient with others — indeed, his patience is the model and the source of ours. Steep your heart in his forgiveness, deal honestly with the cravings under your anger, be slow to speak and quick to forgive, and keep asking for grace. Little by little, the God who is “slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” will make you more like himself — and the peace that grows in a heart set free from anger is one of the sweetest fruits of walking with him. Few changes preach the gospel to the people around us more loudly than a once-angry person become gentle — living proof that God can tame what we could never tame ourselves.
